hook: You know the fruit of the Spirit. But did you know Paul wrote it to churches that were biting and devouring one another?
story:
Paul does not ease into this letter. After a short greeting to “the assemblies of Galatia”, he gets to the point in verse 6: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you”. A few chapters later he calls them “Foolish Galatians”. Bible Odyssey describes the letter as an emotionally charged argument, and it reads that way.

The name Galatia carried a long memory. The province was named for Gauls, Celtic tribes who crossed from Thrace into Asia Minor in the third century before Christ. Three tribes, the Tectosages, the Trocmii and the Tolistobogii, settled the highlands of central Anatolia. Wikipedia dates their arrival to about 278 BC, as raiders and hired soldiers who later settled. Rome annexed the land around 25 BC. The Romans, Bible Odyssey notes, feared the Gauls as fierce and unruly fighters. Whether Paul was writing to the descendants of those Celts, or to towns farther south in the same Roman province, is a question scholars have argued for over a hundred years.

What the letter shows us is the state of the churches. Some people were pressing the non-Jewish believers to be circumcised. Paul answers that “Christ has made us free”, and that they should not be “entangled again with a yoke of bondage”. And the fight had spilled into daily life. In verse 15 he warns them, “if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another”. At the end of the chapter he says “Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.”

In the middle of that stands our verse. Paul has just listed “the deeds of the flesh”, among them “hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions”. Then he turns. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love”. A people who were biting one another are handed a picture of what a community looks like when the Spirit is at work among them.

moment:
Paul is writing to “the assemblies of Galatia”, several churches, not one. He is arguing that these believers are free, and that they should not go back under the law as a way of being right with God. He wants them to hold on to “faith working through love”. At the close he picks up the pen himself: “See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand.”

The readers are not calm. Some are being pushed toward circumcision, and some are turning on each other. Paul says the whole law “is fulfilled in one word”, and the word he gives is love of your neighbor. It is the same love that stands first in the list of fruit.
around:
Just before our verse, Paul tells them to “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh”, and he names the deeds of the flesh as obvious. Just after it he says “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.” Then comes the sentence that holds the passage together: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.”

The verse ends with a short line, “Against such things there is no law.” Paul has spent the letter arguing about law. Here he says that nobody needs a rule against love, joy or peace.
after:
The Bible gives a few later glimpses of these churches. Acts records that Paul went through “the region of Phrygia and Galatia”, and on a later journey he “went through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples.” In a letter to Corinth, Paul writes about a collection for the saints and says he had given the same instruction to “the assemblies of Galatia”. So the churches were still there, and still part of his work. In a later letter he notes that Crescens had gone to Galatia.

The letter itself lasted far longer than the argument. Bible Odyssey says there are no known first-century manuscripts of it, and that the earliest complete copy dates to about 175 to 225. It also records that in the fourth century Jerome claimed the people of Galatia still spoke a Celtic language. Many centuries later Martin Luther wrote a commentary on the whole letter. Paul’s hard letter to a quarrelling people became one of the most quoted in the New Testament.
readings:
The first thing readers notice is that Paul writes fruit, not fruits. In the Luther commentary, love comes first and is said to hold the rest: it would have been enough to name love alone, Luther says, because love embraces all the fruits of the Spirit. On this reading the list is one life seen from nine sides.

A second reading hears each word as a separate trait to grow. Luther walks through them one by one. He describes joy as sweet thoughts of Christ, hymns and thanksgiving, and he is plain about one word. By faith in this list, he says, Paul does not mean faith in Christ but faith in people, a readiness to believe the best of them. That is Luther’s own reading, and he gives it with confidence.

A third question is who the Galatians were. Some scholars place the letter in the Celtic north, others in the southern towns of the same province. Bible Odyssey says the argument rests on how one reads the letter, the Acts of the Apostles and Paul’s chronology. Either way, the verse was written to real churches in real conflict.
point: In this chapter the fruit of the Spirit is set against a community that is biting, provoking and envying. Love comes first in the list, and the same chapter says the whole law is fulfilled in love. The verse describes what a life shaped by the Spirit looks like among other people, not a checklist for a lone believer.
lesson:
If you read this verse as a list of things you should be, it will wear you out, and Paul did not write it that way. He wrote it to people who were hurting each other, and he said that what they needed was not one more rule but the Spirit’s work among them.

So you could read it as a question rather than a score. Which of these nine is hardest for you right now: patience with the person at home, peace in a tense workplace, gentleness with someone who has let you down? Paul does not tell the Galatians to try harder. He tells them to “walk by the Spirit”, and he calls these things fruit, not tasks.

If you want to begin somewhere, read the rest of the chapter and notice what comes before the list and what comes after it. And if you do not share this faith, the picture is still worth keeping: a community known by love, joy and peace instead of biting and envy.

echoes.note: Jesus says that whoever “remains in me and I in him bears much fruit”. The fruit in Galatians grows the same way: from a life joined to him, not from effort alone.
Paul uses the same picture to the church in Ephesus: “the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth”. It is another short list of what the Spirit’s work looks like.
Paul asks believers to wear “a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance”, and says “walk in love”. It lines up with the fruit, and love again comes first.
